reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Pituitary apoplexy is a neuroendocrine emergency caused by sudden haemorrhage or infarction, usually within a pre-existing pituitary adenoma
It presents abruptly with severe headache, visual disturbance, ophthalmoplegia, and often nausea, vomiting, and reduced consciousness
Visual field loss (classically bitemporal from optic chiasm compression) and cranial nerve palsies affecting eye movements arise from expansion into the suprasellar region and cavernous sinus
The most dangerous complication is acute secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency, which can cause life-threatening hypotension and hyponatraemia
Empirical stress-dose corticosteroid cover is a cornerstone of initial management once apoplexy is suspected, before biochemical confirmation delays treatment
MRI is the preferred imaging to demonstrate the pituitary lesion and haemorrhage, as CT may miss subtle changes
Urgent surgical decompression is considered for severe or deteriorating visual loss or reduced consciousness, while selected stable cases may be managed conservatively with close monitoring
Long-term follow-up is needed because many patients develop persistent hormone deficiencies requiring replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Pituitary apoplexy results from acute haemorrhage, infarction, or both within the pituitary gland, most commonly in an existing (often previously undiagnosed) adenoma. Rapid expansion of the gland within the confined sella and suprasellar space compresses adjacent structures: upward pressure on the optic chiasm impairs vision, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus affects the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, and trigeminal branches. Sudden loss of functioning pituitary tissue precipitates hypopituitarism, with acute corticotroph failure being the immediate threat to life. Leakage of blood and necrotic material can also cause meningism.
additionalInvestigations: Urgent MRI of the pituitary and sella to confirm haemorrhage or infarction and assess chiasmal compression
CT head when MRI is unavailable or to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel and serum cortisol before or alongside starting steroids
Serum electrolytes to detect hyponatraemia and monitor for diabetes insipidus
Formal visual acuity and visual field assessment
redFlags: Sudden severe headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia indicating an endocrine and neurosurgical emergency
Haemodynamic instability and hyponatraemia from acute adrenal insufficiency requiring immediate corticosteroids
Rapidly progressive or severe visual field loss needing urgent surgical decompression
Declining conscious level or signs of raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: With prompt corticosteroid cover and, when indicated, timely decompression, visual and neurological recovery is often good; however, permanent hypopituitarism is common and delayed recognition of adrenal crisis can be fatal.
pitfalls: Withholding stress-dose steroids while awaiting hormone results in a suspected case
Relying on CT alone and missing the diagnosis when MRI would reveal the lesion
Mistaking the presentation for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis and delaying endocrine treatment
Failing to arrange long-term endocrine follow-up for evolving hormone deficiencies
management: Give empirical stress-dose intravenous corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone as soon as apoplexy is suspected, to treat life-threatening secondary adrenal insufficiency before biochemical confirmation
Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and correct hyponatraemia and other electrolyte disturbances
Draw a baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel and serum cortisol before or alongside starting steroids, and confirm the diagnosis with urgent pituitary MRI
Refer urgently to neurosurgery for transsphenoidal decompression in patients with severe or progressive visual failure or reduced consciousness
Manage haemodynamically stable patients with intact vision conservatively, with close neurological, visual and endocrine monitoring
Replace deficient hormones long term, including levothyroxine, sex steroids and growth hormone, and monitor for and treat diabetes insipidus with desmopressin
Coordinate care across endocrinology, neurosurgery and ophthalmology with serial visual acuity and field assessment
